name_native: လက်ဖက်သုပ်
processing: Young leaves are steamed or boiled, rolled, packed tightly and fermented without air for weeks to a year to make lahpet so, which is then dressed and tossed with crunchy garnishes.
harvest_season: Commercially, second and third flushes usually go to pickled tea, since the first flush earns more as dried green tea. The earliest leaves make the top grades.
appearance_dry: Not a dry tea: the base is moist, dark olive-green pickled leaf, mixed with fried garlic, peanuts, beans and sesame.
appearance_liquor: None, since it is eaten; it is served beside plain tea, usually a pale yellow-green brew.
appearance_wet: Soft, glistening olive-brown shreds of fermented leaf coated in oil.
taste_profile: Sour, bitter, savoury and spicy at once, with crunch from fried garlic, nuts and beans and a clean, refreshing aftertaste.

brewing.notes: Eaten, not brewed: these numbers are only for the plain green tea served alongside. Dress the pickled leaf with oil, garlic, chilli and lime just before serving.

vintage_note: Not sold by vintage. Pickled tea is sold ready after months to about a year of fermentation, in markets by weight or in kits with garnishes, and is eaten fresh. Golden colour is prized, so some is dyed with turmeric or synthetic colour; a natural olive-brown is nothing to worry about.
description:
Laphet thoke is what most visitors meet first of Myanmar's pickled tea: a salad of fermented tea leaves with fried garlic, peanuts, beans, sesame, chilli and often dried shrimp. It is one of the few cases where tea is food rather than drink, and it is a staple of Burmese hospitality.

The heart of it is lahpet so, wet tea. Leaves are steamed or boiled, rolled, then packed without air in baskets, pits or concrete vats for months. Home makers in Shan State still use bamboo tubes sealed with banana leaf and topped up with water.

Expect sour, bitter and savoury in one mouthful, with the garnishes doing the crunching. It carries a real caffeine kick, and is eaten as a snack as much as a side dish. Serve it with plain green tea.

Quality runs through seven named grades, with young leaf at the top. Prepared kits are the easy way in abroad, but check that the leaf tastes clean and sour rather than simply oily.
history:
Eating pickled tea in this region is very old, a heritage of hill peoples who fermented leaves in bamboo, baskets and pots, and Burmese is among the few languages whose word for tea does not come from Chinese. Folklore credits King Alaungsithu of Pagan with introducing tea in the 1100s; treat that as legend.

As Theravada reform took hold, pickled tea replaced alcohol at ceremonies, and cultivation spread across the northern Shan States after 1500. Lahpet also became a formal gesture: it was exchanged after disputes between kingdoms and eaten after court verdicts to show that they were accepted.

Since the late 2010s, armed conflict in growing areas has disrupted the tea supply.
